items.body: Improvisations for the Land proceeds with unusual patience. Alessandro Ciccarelli and Milena Punzi Anfossi never seem in a hurry to introduce new material. Instead, they linger over individual sounds, allowing them to exhaust their possibilities before searching for another direction. At several points the music appears to reach an impasse, only for one of the musicians to uncover an entirely new path from within the same sonic terrain. The three improvisations share this quality of persistence, probing ever deeper where it might seem there is nothing left to uncover. The relationship between analogue synthesizer and electric cello is one of constant adjustment. Neither instrument occupies a permanent foreground. Sometimes the synthesizer holds a low-frequency plateau almost stubbornly while the cello slowly alters its pressure, grain and register around it. Elsewhere the electronics recede almost completely, leaving bowed textures to define the pace before quietly reclaiming the space through sustained drones and subtle shifts in colour. The music rarely advances through contrast. It moves by patiently examining the consequences of each gesture. Trial-and-error and risk-taking shape the entire album. High frequencies are sometimes sustained long enough to become physically demanding, forcing the listener to remain inside their unsettling presence instead of treating them as fleeting accents. Low drones establish a bodily weight that occasionally feels architectural rather than harmonic. Even when the texture thickens, each sound retains its own presence, allowing the ear to follow the gradual redistribution of energy across the spectrum. Listening repeatedly, one becomes increasingly aware of how carefully the musicians resist resolution. Electronic textures are allowed to stall. Bowed sounds lose energy without being replaced. Instead of smoothing over moments of uncertainty, Ciccarelli and Punzi Anfossi remain with them, allowing hesitation and suspension to become productive musical states. There is a quiet confidence in this willingness to stay with a sound after it has apparently reached its destination. The titles inevitably invite historical associations. Named after Palestinian villages destroyed during the Nakba, the three improvisations carry an emotional and political charge that extends beyond the music itself. Yet, as the musicians explain in the accompanying interview, the names were chosen only after the recordings had been completed. They do not function as narratives but acknowledge a state of mind that accompanied the project. The music retains its autonomy while remaining inseparable from the experiences that shaped its creation. The cover artwork quietly reinforces this idea. Its layered aerial image shows a fractured landscape at different degrees of resolution and density. Surfaces overlap, traces emerge only to disappear beneath new textures, and the eye is left to make sense of the jagged terrain. It mirrors the music’s own behaviour: sounds accumulate through successive layers, preserving earlier gestures without ever allowing them to become fixed. There is no attempt to overwhelm the listener through density or technical display. The album asks for a different kind of attention, one willing to remain inside slowly evolving textures and to follow sounds beyond their apparent destination. The longer one spends with these improvisations, the more they reveal through the patient excavation of what was already there. That patient search gives Improvisations for the Land its own voice. photo by Leonardo Chiarabini – The Factory PRD To explore things further, we have reached out to Alessandro Ciccarelli and Milena Punzi Anfossi. Improvisations for the Land is rooted in free improvisation, yet the album is also explicitly dedicated to Palestine, with each piece named after a village destroyed during the Nakba in 1948. Rather than illustrating specific events, the music seems to inhabit a space of tension, absence, and attentive listening. How did the decision to name the pieces after Isdud, Jusayr, and Hulayqat shape the improvisations themselves? Were you thinking about these places while performing, or did their historical weight become part of the music retrospectively? We believe that instrumental music — and, more specifically, the kind of improvisational practice we pursue — belongs to a process of abstraction in which music both can and should represent nothing but itself, rather than describing or illustrating events, images, or narratives. This autonomy, however, does not justify the notion of an art detached from life. On the contrary, life itself, the events that surround us, and the history we live through inevitably permeate our being, our sensibilities, and our actions as individuals and as musicians. For this reason, although sound does not represent anything, it is never a neutral or sterile space. As John Cage famously said, “Everything we do is music.” The world therefore does not remain outside music; it inevitably enters it through those who create it and those who listen. In his writings on music, Edward Said consistently defended the formal rigor of classical music without ever separating it from his condition as a Palestinian intellectual living in exile. For him, these two dimensions were never in conflict; they coexisted within the same gesture. The autonomy of form does not entail amnesia on the part of those who practice it. With this in mind, the titles of these pieces are neither captions nor interpretative keys, nor do they ask the listener to search within the music for references to a place or event. In her essay “Against Interpretation,” Susan Sontag argued that interpretation can become a way of taming a work of art — reducing it to its content and then interpreting that, making it manageable. At a time when criticism tended to approach every work as something to decode, the first question became, “What does it mean?”— as though its value lay in some hidden message waiting to be extracted and restated elsewhere. For Sontag, this is precisely what taming means: neutralizing what is intrinsic to a work, what cannot be reduced to a concept, in order to render it harmless. At bottom, this is what she calls “the philistine refusal to leave the work of art alone.” Interpretation risked extinguishing the immediate, sensory impact that a work has on those who hear or see it — an experience that is essential and prior to any content one might later extract from it. We therefore conceive these titles not as content to be extracted from the music, but as biographical traces of ourselves. They do not assign meaning to the listening experience; rather, they point to those who made the music. The decision to title and dedicate these pieces to villages destroyed during the Nakba came only afterward, once the music already existed, but not in order to impose an external meaning upon it. Rather, it was an acknowledgment that those improvisations had already been traversed by our own anxieties, by the anger and grief we felt in the face of the unspeakable. The title does not explain the music; it names the condition of those who created it. Isdud 1930 In the liner notes you write that, while art cannot stop violence, it also cannot remain isolated from the world. That raises a broader question about artistic responsibility. When working on an entirely improvised album, how do you negotiate the relationship between political intention and musical openness? Were there moments where you felt the music itself resisted the conceptual framework you had established, or did improvisation become precisely the right language for responding to events that seem almost impossible to represent? Free improvisation is probably the musical practice in which the performer’s life, emotions, thoughts, and memories enter the musical act most directly. Not by narrating events, but by allowing the sound itself to reveal a presence of one’s inner world that precedes any explanation. Unlike composed music, the outcome of improvisation is always bound to the hic et nunc of the self, and of the self in relation to the other. The environment, one’s state of mind, one’s thoughts, and interpersonal relationships are all integral to the construction of the music. They do not constitute an external context; they are among the very materials of improvisation. For Christopher Small, music is not so much an object as a shared activity — a process of musicking that encompasses performers, listeners, and the relationships that emerge between them in the moment of performance. If there is a political dimension, it is enacted within this network of relationships that comes into being every time people make music together. Pauline Oliveros described Deep Listening as the practice of “listening in every possible way to everything possible to hear.” For us, this means that improvisation is not merely about producing sounds, but about assuming the responsibility of being fully present: listening to one another, to the space, and to the world. It is a mode of listening that precedes expressive intention and also entails a willingness to be transformed by whatever unfolds. For this reason, we have never experienced any tension between political commitment and musical openness. As we suggested earlier, lived experience inevitably enters the sound itself, and precisely for that reason we believe free improvisation is the language best suited to engaging with events that exceed every possibility of representation. Faced with tragedies of this magnitude, music neither can nor should claim to narrate, explain, or stand in for history. What it can do is become a space in which such experiences continue to question both those who perform and those who listen. According to Jacques Rancière, the politics of art does not reside in the message it conveys, but in the way it reconfigures the distribution of the sensible — that is, what can be seen, heard, and shared. In a complementary sense, Jacques Attali argued that music is prophecy: rather than merely reflecting society, it heralds forms that have not yet become visible elsewhere, in a movement he calls annunciatory. If this is true, then a record such as this does not simply “comment” on tragedy through its titles. Rather, in the very way it is organized and experienced, it attempts to imagine a different configuration of reality. For this reason, we do not believe in the possibility of neutral art. The autonomy of music does not mean isolation from history. Every sonic gesture emerges within a network of relationships, experiences, and responsibilities. In this sense, it is not so much that music “speaks about politics”; rather, sound itself, as a human gesture situated in the world, inevitably possesses a political dimension. Sound is political. Hulayqat 1940s map Compared to your previous duo album All’improvviso, the instrumentation here has been reduced to its bare essentials: electric cello and analogue synthesizer. Yet that apparent limitation produces an extraordinarily rich sonic vocabulary, where it often becomes difficult to distinguish which sounds belong to the cello and which emerge from the synthesizer. How has your musical dialogue evolved since your first collaboration, and what possibilities did this more austere instrumental setup open up for both of you? We both share the need to constantly question ourselves and to explore new ways of discovering sound within sound. This happens both individually, through our own personal research, and collectively in our work as a duo. By “new means” we do not simply refer to different devices or instruments, as was the case with our first album, All’Improvviso, but also to new expressive possibilities that emerge from a deeper exploration of each instrument itself. Sometimes, innovation does not come from adding new elements, but from looking more deeply at what is already available to us and questioning our habitual ways of using it. Our decision to reduce the instrumentation to an electric cello and an analogue synthesizer was therefore not an act of renunciation, but part of this very process: a way of focusing our attention on sonic material itself. Limiting our means — both in terms of instruments and musical materials — has never felt like a constraint. On the contrary, it creates a deeper space for exploration, where every timbral variation, every resonance, and every subtle detail acquires greater significance. Giacinto Scelsi spoke of the profondeur du son — the depth of sound — conceiving sound not merely as a vehicle for music but as an autonomous universe to be explored in its own internal complexity. From this perspective, our interest is not simply in combining the electric cello and the analogue synthesizer as two distinct instruments, but in exploring the point at which their identities begin to dissolve and sound becomes a shared space, a material in continuous transformation. This exploration unfolds through a process of exchange and reciprocity, ideally reaching a point where the distinction between the two sound sources no longer matters. The fact that it is often difficult to tell whether a particular sound originates from the cello or the synthesizer is therefore not merely the result of each of us pursuing our own timbral research. Rather, it is the outcome of an encounter between two depths: both instruments become generators of a shared sonic material, continuously transformed through listening, interaction, and mutual responsiveness. Jusair 1940s map Listening to Improvisations for the Land, I was struck by how much the music relies on restraint. Silence, resonance, and microscopic changes in timbre often carry as much expressive weight as the more overt musical gestures, while the dialogue between electric cello and analogue synthesizer unfolds with remarkable patience and responsiveness. At many points it becomes difficult to tell where one instrument ends and the other begins, as both seem to inhabit the same evolving sonic space. How do you cultivate that degree of mutual listening during improvisation? Is it something that develops over years of playing together, or do you deliberately create conditions that allow unexpected musical relationships to emerge in the moment? Although a musical relationship can certainly be built and deepened over time through shared experience and growing familiarity, there are also rare encounters in which something seems to happen immediately, before words and without the need for any particular preparation. These are the moments when a musical dialogue emerges from the very first sound, as a form of mutual recognition. That epiphany is exactly what happened the first time we played together as a duo. All’improvviso, our first album, grew out of that experience: a first meeting, with no rehearsal, no predetermined structures, and no direction established in advance. We simply brought our willingness to listen and to respond to whatever unfolded in the present moment. Ever since that first encounter, we have had the feeling that our shared sound has always found its own continuity, its own direction, while remaining completely open. Of course, this sense of affinity does not imply the absence of research or risk. On the contrary, within such a deep mode of listening, the unexpected becomes an essential source of creative energy. What we do not know is not an obstacle but an opportunity for transformation. Improvisation ultimately lives within this tension between familiarity and the unknown. Writing about non-idiomatic improvisation, Derek Bailey argued that the value of this practice lies precisely in not knowing in advance what will happen. It is not defined by the absence of an idiom, but by the decision to relinquish any pre-existing idiom in order to remain in the position of discovering something together with another person. We recognize the foundation of our own listening to one another in that condition, more than in any acquired technique. For us, improvisation means exposing ourselves to the risk of losing what we already know, accepting that control can never be total, and allowing space for something that can emerge only through the relationship itself. It is precisely this dimension of risk that keeps the musical dialogue alive and vital. In this sense, listening is not simply the ability to follow the other; it is also the willingness to allow the other to change the course of our own path. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: With the completion of this trilogy, we acknowledge our part as a remote viewer of Dean’s life over three decades. Salvaging The Future—perhaps more than the prior two albums—is a restless collage, yet it is so well mixed that it lends itself to uninterrupted full-album listening. This listener is tuning in about 2x per day at the moment. Despite the challenges these decades have wrought, the trilogy’s close with “Our Story Survives Collectively” leaves us with a sense of hope. This is music for visioning. Revolutionizing the human listening experience Salvaging The Future by Dean De Benedictis Salvaging the Future utilizes electronic mastery alongside sparse traditional acoustic instruments and vocals to revolutionize the human listening experience. There will be no undisturbed sleeping, only optional vivid, deep-set dreaming. Music that completely upends your expectations can feel like a sensory assault on the first spin, but the feeling soon becomes mostly energizing and sustaining, including a wispy blend of limitless and beatless space signatures, as well as beat inspired enchantment. This is Art, intending to allow the unconscious mind to somehow express itself, often resulting in the depiction of illogical or dreamlike scenes and ideas. “Moving forward with mindfulness would quite literally mean salvaging the future,” offers De Benedictis. We may expect The Future to bring about profound changes in our listening arts through universal joyfulness, mindful that nothing is forever. As for dancing, that is up to you. I seek a collage shifting into every new world imaginable, or mostly never before imagined. Southern California-based artist Dean De Benedictis has delivered an absolute masterpiece for your collection of auditory journeys that completely bypass conventional reason and transport your mind into uncharted, supernatural territories. He ​is widely recognized in the electronic ambient community as Surface 10. Surface 10 has a long history with performing at galactic electronic music festivals as well as releasing his solo and collaborative recordings internationally, such as on the DiN label, Hypnotic, Space For Music, as well as some self-released works. His previous work with Spotted Peccary Music includes a collaborative project called Desensitized, with Deborah Martin (Hemispherica Portalis, 2020, and Chaos In Premonition, 2022) as well as two solo albums, Salvaging the Past (2005) and Salvaging the Present (2016). Only optional vivid, deep-set dreaming :: Salvaging the Future presents an attempt to conceive and apply a good degree of futurism to every aspect of its creation. From sound design, to instrumentation, to compositional production, perhaps one way to see it (or hear it) is as an illusive combination of progressive and contemporary influences that all “tap the future on the shoulder” or if nothing else, maybe exchange a hat-tip to that which is to come. Additionally, the obvious suggestion that humanity’s future may still have hope for survival and even thriving; that we may somehow redeem and persevere not by forgetting or dismissing our weight of the past, but acknowledging and accounting for life experiences as a strategy for our progress ahead. “Aside from representing phases of my life, the Salvaging series began as one idea, and ended as another,” confides De Benedictis. “The musical style of Salvaging The Future follows the suggestion of its inherent theme: a wild departure from most past and current genres, diving head first into hyper-forward approaches, perhaps in some ways “of the future.” “I would produce and perform music in harsh desert planes, steep canyons, mountainsides and summits, windswept shores and forested wilderness; I would work in abandoned buildings, housing construction, airplane flights, cafes, hotels, museums, libraries, or while staying with friends, family, or indeed at home, which was most of the time even if not by far. I tended to do a lot of re-synth types of methods, so found sounds combined with both customized sample libraries and Apple libraries were yet again the main source of instrumentation on Salvaging The Future, much like Salvaging The Present.” Also, like Salvaging The Present, there was an immense amount of processor stacking and automation, mountains of hardware, on every instrument track. “Featured on both albums was also a customized library of drum hits I created in 2014, in which each hit captures the reverb trail-from a note (or harmony) that was sung just before it. This hit library formulated a fairly unmistakable signature-sound in most of my work that followed. I still use that custom-drum-hits library to this day. However, unlike Salvaging The Present, which was completely produced on only one laptop, Salvaging The Future was composed on my first two laptops as well as my first tower. It was all old Apple gear and software, but for some reason that still sounded better to me than some of my newer gear and software, so I decided to just accept the old-system setbacks and finish the album on those devices regardless. A wild departure from most past and current genres :: “It almost broke me. I had to deal with endless system complications on every device, prompting constant work-arounds with Logic and Ableton, but the sound made it worthwhile for me.” De Benedictis continues his long, internationally recognized history of stripping ordinary objects of their normal significance to expose deep psychological truths. By tying an essential common thread between opposing genres, he has created an abstract, emotionally rich masterwork that demands to be heard for fans of avant-garde electronic exploration. Salvaging the Future was composed, performed, mixed, edited, designed and conceptualized by Dean De Benedictis between 2010 and 2025, using mostly software on laptops. His additional instruments were flute, voice, piano and guitar. Production locations were scattered throughout the US west coast but based primarily in Thousand Oaks and Santa Monica, CA. Contributing extra recorded musicians, in addition to Apple loops, include: Lara De Benedictis (vocals), D’Von Charley (vocals and native flute), Nichole Michelle Jones (vocals), Lisa Claire Mitterer (vocals), Phil Williams (electric guitar), and various ASMR artists. ASMRtists. Autonomous Sensory Meridian Response (ASMR) and Ray Kersweil’s futurist theory of the Singularity are two unrelated ideas I came across while researching this music, both have been popular but I have never before heard of them, so kudos. ASMR seems to explore some of the physical psychology of sound. The Kersweil concepts are set in the future, during the coming singularity, and all planets and celestial bodies are now shifting and morphing and changing as that same singularity. This revolutionary sonic journey begins abruptly with “My Love Is An Extinction Event” (6:10), a track whose song title invokes the concept of a rapid, widespread drop in biodiversity. Here things come together and things come apart and sometimes this happens at the same time, spinning and bouncing, falling and transferring velocity, which feels bizarre, unbelievable, dreamlike and leads into very strange restless ear-born images. The kind that will change your life. At one moment the mood goes from feeling frenetic to feeling incredibly alive and layered. This unexpected salad of situations, places, or emotional moments that seem detached from everyday reality or logic all feel pretty good, the intimate links between freeing imagination and the mind, and liberation from repressive and archaic social structures. In the beginning, deep space has no beat. Welcome to “The Outer Links”  (6:31). Coming from an intentionally beatless expanse designed to liberate the imagination, giving the listener the sensation of flying through colorful lights, and maneuvering deliberately to liberate the imagination. We are flying along at a more rapid speed now. The feeling is all about bright stars and a sense of transit. Soon everything is almost flying apart and the beat is going at a fast clip. As the album progresses, we encounter “Voca”  (3:35), where small pieces suddenly click and morph into a fast-paced, jamming run driven by a sexy bassline and seasonably hot drum tones. Perhaps the tempo is a bit fidgety but always rich in tone and interesting in context, jumping into many places to tell the story. I do not understand the punchline, but even real life itself can be strange and even uncomfortable when seeking sustenance. Music for visioning :: I think the fourth track starts in a calm memory palace illuminated with tall marble columns, with big bright halls and stairways. Soon a beat contraption comes together and the vocalists start to arrive. “They Fought To Sway” (7:18) is my personal favorite here, the vocals reach a place I have never heard before, and I like that. “Urband Glacier Fund”  (6:27) is probably holding a hidden message, leading to speculation about that extra d in Urband. Hidden portals bring delight, I think that we are in outer space coming upon some new life forms, our synthesizers are carefully subtle and fully capable. Now a new beat arrives and takes over, a new darkness has surrounded the cabin. Are there glaciers in outer space? The flute is here to take us along, with amazing high energy. Now we encounter a big cinematic sly beat and things are happening all over the place, very exciting. “ASMR Tragedy Lines” (6:44) seems to take place down in a very deep tunnel or cavern, robots are building things quietly, except for this one guy. It gets extremely quiet out here, where we are in the cavern. The perception distorts, morphs, and transforms ordinary objects and forms into strange and uncanny variations of themselves. Down there something is always sparkling. Now the whispers in the darkness take over. I keep straining to hear what the voices are planning next. The imaginary narrative shifts beautifully on “Salvaging My Story” (7:12), a track full of radiant stars, choirs, and unexpected juxtapositions that exercise the grand element of surprise. Let’s go out into the fields at night where the space ships will land, be sure to keep an eye out. There are steam powered machines running, there are crickets and I expect to find the children of the night out here. Soon there is a change. There is a shy melodic tune lingering in the caverns along with the choirs and radiant stars. Soon all of the details start coming into focus, this is a big story with plenty of flying at night. Away we are going, exercising the element of surprise, unexpected juxtapositions and non sequitur. It works. This leads right into the slow-burning sunrise of “Future Incandescence” (6:32) which unfolds like a long slow transit in deep space. Now the pace is slower and the feeling is starker, disorienting, with the hallucinatory quality of a dream. There is a language of fragments that flow together and make the whole sound. We are still on the ship, snug inside a safe metal box that is still moving, the closest star is emerging from an eclipse, there are emotions and suspense, there is tension building. The natural world takes a surreal turn on “All The Wild” (4:27), where there are strange gumblings coming from animals that I cannot see. We are all probably back in the big cave again, at night. This time with strange recordings of birds and wildlife playing in the darkness. The variety of strange sounds increases as new species come floating into our range. There are a lot of creatures heard here, such as birds or lizards cooing, insects clicking and humming. I think I hear a synth glowing, perhaps a swan, with pianos and choirs and sustained tones echoing about. Some loons explode or just fly ahead, and there are more new strange creatures. There are whales in our cave here, along with the strings and wings. “Born Of Flight” (7:09) starts in quiet secrecy before combusting into a galloping drum kit that soon clicks like a flying train, keeping the listener in a state of perpetual, blissful motion. We love our cave, it goes on forever. By the end we are clicking like a sleeping railroad carriage, always feeling motion, until we gently float into the close. The album concludes with a magnificent nine-minute epic, “Our Story Survives Collectively” (9:15), and to start we are following our guide into the well lit tunnel or hallway, there are echoes and lots of space above. There are interesting odd vocals, some with a trilling vibrato. Now for me there was suddenly a grand design to the whole program. I could see that there are complimentary combinations of elements and a thriving life force, and we are all together. Salvaging The Future by Dean De Benedictis   Dean De Benedictis is a Southern California-based artist who has always utilized his interest in a variety of styles and cultures to enrich the quality of his musical expression. He aspires to communicate a similar functionality for the experiences of his listeners. Deans’ music is the result of his will to tie an essential common thread together between opposing genres and mentalities, as well as draw from them a natural sense of emotion, expanse and mystery. Sound exposes psychological truth; stripping ordinary objects of their normal significance, to create a compelling image that is beyond ordinary formal organization, in order to evoke empathy from the listener, with a combination of the depictive, the abstract, and the psychological.Driving into the complex, shape-shifting worlds that De Benedictis creates is always a magnificent adventure. He juxtaposes those frantic, glitchy granular textures against massive, cinematic spaces, sometimes he drops a rogue flute solo or harmonica right into a heavy electronic beat. It’s the kind of music that feels less like a collection of songs and more like a living, breathing, possibly dangerous ecosystem; De Benedictis has created an abstract, emotionally rich soundscape universe that rewards the listener.“My Salvaging trilogy of albums was a sincere and perhaps far-flung attempt to tie a form of common thread between the periods of my life and the electronic music I never released during those periods. Naturally, the reoccurring concept and eventual theme of ‘salvaging time’ manifested into the project. I basically have boxes filled with music like this, built up through decades. As such, my Salvaging trilogy was only one of many projects with a similar goal – to salvage works of the past – but the Salvaging Trilogy itself might be my most qualitative among them.“There are some very clear differences in style and approach contrasting each of these three albums, but it’s really the difference between the first album and the two albums following that one where the contrast is most visible. My first Salvaging album in 2005, Salvaging The Past, was a collection of work created throughout the ‘90s in my home studio, where I was surrounded by physical synthesizers and racks of outboard gear. Sometime between that album and the next one, Salvaging The Present, I acquired my first laptop and lots of appropriate software (more laptops would soon follow).“This changed the game, and my life, in ways that I couldn’t have imagined years earlier. I was already a traveler and an outdoorsman, so suddenly having the power to virtually access an entire studio within a little portable box was very liberating, conceptually and literally. I ended up travelling far and wide with the music, albeit mostly within US borders, but still found myself creating spontaneous productions in some of America’s most extreme natural environments. Over a period of about a decade-and-a-half, I lived a separate little lifetime of fair adventure with these devices, even including some uncomfortable brushes with death.“This spanned the length of both concurrent albums after the first one, I endured to keep creating through massive amounts of life changes and personal upheaval; through each new home I found, whether on-the-road or stationary; through broken alliances and rock-and-jazz-band breakups; through family drama and harddrive thefts and accidental overdoses, and of course a pandemic. Even through it all, my personal standard of innovation-balanced-by-emotional-sincerity never faltered, which probably explains the long lapses between Salvaging albums.“My desire to musically attempt going where no man or woman had gone before, both sonically and musically, remained. Everything from my sound-design methods to my processing methods to my performing and editing methods, was all totally signature, through every twist and turn and every new resolution. I suppose that’s what’s most noticeable and even distinguishable about this last and final album of the trilogy, Salvaging The Future; it’s the one with the biggest complexities and most contrasting styles, because my desire for balance between cutting-edge method and emotional sincerity were still unwavering through even the most tumultuous period of my life.”It is only natural, after all, to keep pace with scientific and industrial progress as well as follow the lure of pure psychic automatism, to stand for transforming the alienation which many people feel in the modern period, combined with the sense of reaching more deeply into the psyche, to be made whole with one’s individuality.With the completion of this trilogy, we acknowledge our part as a remote viewer of Dean’s life over three decades. Salvaging The Future—perhaps more than the prior two albums—is a restless collage, yet it is so well mixed that it lends itself to uninterrupted full-album listening. This listener is tuning in about 2x per day at the moment. Despite the challenges these decades have wrought, the trilogy’s close with “Our Story Survives Collectively” leaves us with a sense of hope. This is music for visioning. Salvaging The Future is available on Spotted Peccary Music. items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — Sticking together for one more album, Roger Sutton's Riff Raff pull off another very cool Jazz Rock album--something edging its way into the Canterbury conversation. Perhaps working in Kent (where Canterbury lies) with producer Ken Burgess (who would go on to work with Tommy Eyre's next band, Zzebra) had something to do with that.1. "Original Man" (7:40) this Peter Kirtley composition opens with a one minute whole band intro that borders on sounding like something from one of their Canterbury contemporaries, but then in the second minute things settle down into a very cool almost downtempo ambient electric lounge music over which Peter sings in a bit of a Dylanesque style. Peter's lead guitar play in the middle portends the coming of Stevie Ray Vaughan as well as paying a bit of an homage to his contemporary, Eric Clapton. What a great, powerful song to open an album with! Signs of good things to come! (14.375/15)2. "Havakak" (6:06) another really cool Jazz-Rock Fusion song that sounds like something National Health or The Soft Machine would have done. There is just such a great warmth to the feel of this palette and the soundscape it creates: no matter if the band is ripping through it (first motif), slowing things down (second motif), blues-rocking it (third motif), or vamping for Peter Kirtley's extended solo (fourth motif), the sound just wraps around you and makes you feel a part of it. And to think it was a composition that Peter brought from working with keyboard master Kenny Craddock and bassist Colin Gibson during their Mark-Almond days! (9.75/10)3. "Goddamm the Man" (6:09) a Roger Sutton original places us in a juke joint in the Louisiana/Mississippi swamp as raw steel-string acoustic guitars pick away Jack Johnson style from both the left and right while Roger's funky bass and Aureo's drums and congas and Tommy Eyre's stanky electric piano and organ add and increase the funky stink (everybody seems to have taken on at least two tracks). I didn't think I was going to like this once it opened (especially with Roger's Swamp-style American White Blues vocals) but once it got going, once the background vocals and horn section's accents were added, the funk just took over: I'm a fan! (9.25/10)4. "In the Deep" (3:59) Oh, my gosh! Is Robert Wyatt in the house? Peter Kirtley's second offering to the album finds us deep in the forlorn ballad forms that reluctantly came out of the Canterbury Scene. There is so much funky R&B in this--and it feels so solid and natural! Every nuance and subtlety injected, added, and feels so perfect, so genius, so easy! Shades of two of the best to ever do this style: Paddy McAloon (Prefab Sprout) and Roddy Frame (Aztec Camera) as well as the contemporary master extemporaneosifier, Richard Sinclair. Awesome and alarmingly good! (9.75/10)5. "The Waster" (5:09) feels a bit like a continuation or variation on a palette, pace, and style used in all of the previous songs (the sound French downtempo band AIR mastered for their massive hit, >). Roger Sutton's second composition finds him drifting more into the singing style of Eric Burdon (think "Drink This Wine"; even the lyrical format is very much like that iconic song). I love the laid-back vibe of the musicians' spacious note and chord play, a late night application of funk. Horn accents, smooth Fender Rhodes, congas and drums, background vocals, bluesy rhythm guitar, lead sax in the instrumental section, nice, easy-going two-chord construct (think Traffic's "Feelin' Alright"). It's nice, it's fun, it's warm, it's equally well performed as the album's previous material, just a little more tranquilizing. (8.875/10)6. "Tom's Song" (4:22) the title, of course, referring to keyboardist Tommy Eyre, who is the composer of this song. Though it starts out having a little trouble defining itself and its melodies for the first minute, it eventually metes out some quite lovely music: the piano playing and synth strings support quite lush and romantic. Roger's bass and Aureo's congas are muted into the background leaving the synth strings, piano, voice, and Steve Gregory's weirdly-effected flutes in the foreground. Tom's vocal is rather gentle, doubled up, I think. It's obviously a sad love song about regret. I like it's edgy classical and jazz influences as well as Tom's genuine emotion. (9/10)7. "Speed" (9:16) another great construct from multiple influences: the funky blues, American Southern Rock, Traffic, The Allman Brothers, and a little Van Morrison and The Doors in the mix. Another Roger Sutton original, I consider this to be not a particularly great or memorable "epic" but definitely another serious and high quality rendering. (17.625/20)Total Time 42:41It feels weird to be categorizing music coming from Great Britain with labels like "Southern Rock," "Swamp Rock" or "American Southern Rock" but they would not be the only British artists attracted to those types of American sounds. (Think of Alan Parker's film The Commitments and its characters' connection to the Memphis Horns and the music of Wilson Pickett.) Almost every British artist who was coming of age in the early 1960s would cite American Blues, Soul, R&B, and even Jazz as essential foundations and inspirations for their music. Roger Sutton, Peter Kirtley, Tommy Eyre, and Bud Beadle would be no different. I do, however, give the band credit for hearing and emulating a bit of their own countrymates of the Canterbury Style.A/five stars; an eclectic and full-blown masterpiece of sophisticated and highly-nuanced original music by some sadly-under-appreciated musicians (and band). HIGHLY recommended to any professed and self-respecting music lover.

items.body: Review by VianaProghead — Review N� 983"The Singles Collection Volume 1" is a compilation album of Queen that was released in 2008. It has tracks from all the first seven studio albums of the band. So, it has three tracks from "Queen" from 1973, one track from "Queen II" from 1974, five tracks from "Sheer Heart Attack" also from 1974, five tracks from "A Night At The Opera" from 1975, five tracks from "A Day At The Races" from 1976, four tracks from "News Of The World" from 1977 and four tracks from "Jazz" from 1978. It has also a non-album's track, a track that was previously unreleased on any of these studio albums."The Singles Collection Volume 1" has twenty-eight tracks. So, from "Queen" we have "Keep Yourself Alive", "Son And Daughter" and "Seven Seas Of Rhye". "Keep Yourself Alive" is an energetic piece, a straight forward rock song with different and unexpected changes in tempo, with great guitar and vocal work. "Son And Daughter" is a great hard rock song that proves Queen could make hard rock with quality and some progressive lines. "Seven Seas Of Rhye" is an instrumental track. Despite be a short piece is a beautiful song. From "Queen II" we have "White Queen (As It Began)". It's an acoustic ballad with a dark atmosphere, great lyrics, a nice melody, a great guitar solo and a good arrangement. From "Sheer Heart Attack" we have "Killer Queen", "Flick Of The Wrist", "Now I'm Here", "Lily Of The Valley" and "Tenement Funster". "Killer Queen" is a sophisticated and pompous art rock song with great vocals and chorus. It's one of their best songs. "Flick Of The Wrist" is a great track with nice vocals, excellent guitar work with an inspired riff. "Now I'm Here" is a song specially noted for its hard riff and great vocal harmonies. It's a powerful rock number with a heavy beat and catchy vocals. "Lily Of The Valley" is a short song with a nice melody that skills the great capabilities of Mercury as a songwriter. "Tenement Funster" is a good rock number with a heavy tune. It's one of the best Taylor's compositions, one who had stood better the test of time. From "A Night At The Opera" we have "Bohemian Rhapsody", "I'm In Love With My Car", "You're My Best Friend", "'39" and "Death On Two Legs (Dedicated To...)". "Bohemian Rhapsody" is one of the most known and the best songs of Queen. It's one of the greatest rock songs too. "I'm In Love With My Car" is a great rock song, simple and catchy. It's one of Taylor's best songs in Queen's catalogue. "You're My Best Friend" is a beautiful and catchy song with nice harmonies. "'39" is a superb acoustic ballad with great guitar work and beautiful harmonies. "Death On Two Legs (Dedicated To...)" is a great rock song with good harmonies, nice piano, amazing lyrics and a great vocal work. From "A Day At The Races" we have "Somebody To Love", "White Man", "Tie Your Mother Down", "You And I" and "Good Old Fashioned Lover Boy". "Somebody To Love" is a song with some complex harmonies and guitar solos and an incredible gospel choir too. "White Man" is a great hard rock song with excellent musical structure, strong melodies and guitar riffs, one of their heaviest tracks. "Tie Your Mother Down" is a good hard rock guitar based oriented song where May shines. "You And I" is a very simple beautiful song where the arrangements and performance of all band's members are great. "Good Old Fashioned Lover Boy" is one of the several music-hall inspired songs of Queen. It shows their humorous side. From "News Of The World" we have "We Are The Champions", "We Will Rock You", "Spread Your Wings" and "Sheer Heart Attack". "We Are The Champions" is one of the rock most recognizable anthems, even in our days. It's simply an amazing track. "We Will Rock You" is a great rock song that soon became one of the best known and most popular songs of Queen. "Spread Your Wings" is a beautiful rock ballad with good guitar harmonies. It's one of Deacon's better contributions to Queen. "Sheer Heart Attack" is a heavy punk rock song, probably the heaviest song that Queen ever wrote. From "Jazz" we have "Bicycle Race", "Fat Bottomed Girls", "Don't Stop Me Now" and "In Only Seven Days". "Bicycle Race" is a great song with an unusual chord progression with several modulations and multi-tracked vocals and guitar harmonies. "Fat Bottomed Girls" is a good rock song with an open tuning guitar riff based in blues and hard rock. It has also a great choral work. "Don't Stop Me Now" is a great song with great quality. It's one of their most popular songs even today. "In Only Seven Days" is a nice song with a good melody, good chorus and good musical atmosphere. "See What A Fool I've Been" is a non-album's track. It wasn't released on "Queen II". It was only released as the B-side of their single "Seven Seas Of Rhye".Conclusion: As its name indicates this is a compilation album only with tracks that were released as singles. This isn't a strange thing. As we all know, Queen was always a single's band with the releases of an amount of them. By the other hand, Queen never was a band with lengthy tracks. It has only singles that were released from their first seven studio albums. These are singles that belong to their best and most progressive phase. And I think it's peaceful to say the five first studio albums of the band have many progressive lines and the majority of the tracks that appear on "The Singles Collection Volume 1" were taken from those five albums. So, we can say this is a good compilation album of Queen.Prog is my Ferrari. Jem Godfrey (Frost*)

items.body: The Greek duo—comprising George Katsanos and Irini Tiniakou—formed their musical alter ego, Incirrina, in Athens in 2017. This year, they released their third full-length album, “Trace”, via the German label Cold Transmission Music. Over the years, their sound and influences have steadily evolved from Dark-Wave towards a style leaning more towards Minimal/Electro-Wave, featuring Irini’s icy vocals. The result is a distinctive soundscape that evokes a sense of 1980s nostalgia through its cold analogue tones. I caught up with the duo for an entertaining and informative chat, and they left a lasting impression on me—not only as passionate artists, but also as incredibly kind and appreciative people. (Courtesy by Inferno Sound Diaries) Q: “Trace” is already your third full-length album. Looking back on everything you’ve achieved so far, how do you view your journey as a band? And how would you describe and introduce this new record to people who may not have heard it yet? George: Indeed, after the releases of the albums “8.15” (2019) and “Lip Led Scream” (2022), we are happy to have our third LP “Trace” out by the label Cold Transmission, released 29.5.2026. We consider the band as a space for exploration, experimentation, personal expression, also as an inner journey and diving into our souls. Incirrina has brought us the joy of sharing our music with people across multiple countries. Until now we have toured in 12 European countries and played in many gigs and Festivals, which led to beautiful and completely new experiences. Irini: In this album, we experimented with instrumentation, rhythm and vocal approach. We used a combination of analogue synthesizers, drum machines, octapad, electric bass guitar, electric piano and acoustic instruments such as kantele, waterphone, melodica. “Trace” includes 11 songs written between 2023-2025 in a 24-channel console, that belong in the genres of Dark-Electronic, Synth-Wave and Cold-Wave. The Minimal-Synth and Post-Punk roots of our previous albums are still obvious, yet the new songs are enriched with dynamism, depth, and rhythmic diversity and we also explored new ways of delivering the vocals for this album. Also we would like to note that this album is the result of the collaboration of many people who put their heart and talent into it, and we are grateful to them -these people are Dimitris Dimitriadis (mixing), Anestis Psaradakos (mastering), uBuDancer (ArtWork-AnalogueCollage), Nestor Theophilopoulos (photography), Maria Deligiorgi/Infrared Media (Layout) and Suzy Hermann and Andreas Hermann of Cold Transmission. Q: If I’m not mistaken, you’ve been active for almost ten years now. How did Incirrina come into being, and how have both your collaboration and the band itself evolved over the years? George: Our common journey as Incirrina started in late 2017. Since both of us are professional musicians and music teachers, we’ve been involved in numerous bands and projects and music has always been the center of our lives, but neither of us had ever been in a purely synth band before. It was a great pleasure to discover already in our first meeting, in September 2014, that we had the exact same taste in music- we were talking for hours about Jean Michel Jarre, Joy Division, The Cure, Kraftwerk and numerous others… We became a couple, still the timing for forming a band wasn’t right yet- we were working hard in teaching and the other projects, and simply didn’t have the time to start something new together. But in 2017 life brought things together in such a way that conditions were created for something new to be born. Incirrina came into life with the aim to make music in the style we’ve deeply loved since we were teenagers. Irini: The first tracks were written right in our living room. Although I do write lyrics, we chose to base our songs on the poetry of William Blake, an artist we both deeply adore. After recording 6 songs, and without thinking twice, we uploaded them on Bandcamp (this was the first EP “8.15”; in December 2018), and suddenly something clicked. We received an unexpected wave of enthusiasm from complete strangers. Essentially, we started with no expectations other than making songs that we liked. It was magical how this evolved. One year later, in late 2019, the Greek label Geheimnis Records released “8.15” as an LP -the first 6 songs plus 5 new ones. Then COVID hit. During those strange years of isolation, we wrote the songs for our second album, “Lip Led Scream”, which was released by Cold Transmission in August 2022. One thing naturally led to another; some months before the lockdown, we had received an invitation to perform in Germany, in Slow Club Freiburg, a show that finally came to life in May 2022. That was the spark that started this beautiful adventure of European tours and live shows. In the years leading up to this year’s release of “Trace”, we focused on live performances as well as exploring new sounds and we also scored two theatrical plays in Athens. We are quite strict with our music , even though we compose new tracks very quickly, the ones we choose to release are very few (for every track we release, about four or five others are left behind). George: We really enjoy jamming and playing together, most of our tracks come alive through this very process. But there are also songs written entirely by one of us, then the other one enriched or reshaped them, regarding arrangement or structure. While we co-write the harmonic and melodic elements of our songs and handle the arrangements together, our individual roles are quite distinct. I focus on the rhythmic side, taking care of the live drums and drum programming, also the basslines and the riffs, while Irini handles the vocals. Q: One of the defining characteristics of your music is your use of analogue synthesizers. That seems like a very deliberate choice. What is it about analogue synths that continues to inspire you, and how has this aspect of your sound evolved over the years, particularly on “Trace”? George: Indeed, we have a great love for analog sound and analog synthesizers. Of course, there are plenty digital instruments we really like and also use. I adore Moog synthesizers, their rich harmonic sound fills the ear with very distinct frequencies. I love that you can never have the exact same sound. The instruments that I use do not have a ‘preset’ or ‘save’ possibility, so every time I make the sound from the beginning and I find this really thrilling. Analog synthesizers have personality; I feel like I’m using a sonic canvas when playing them, their sound has so many shades and details. Irini: We’ve used analog synths on all of our albums. In “Trace”, we paired them with acoustic instruments and also some digital synths, like the AKAI MPC and the Yamaha PS-55. Even though the Yamaha is digital, it’s from way back in 1983, and its sound has this nostalgic warmth that really speaks to us. Our relationship with instruments is just like with people… we have great chemistry and love for some, while others we just can’t connect with at all! An instrument is a whole world of its own, and a single sound can inspire an entire song. Some tracks started out just from a single sound, like the song “She Is In The Dream”. We also love building lots of layers and textures when it comes to orchestration, and our analog synths are perfect for mixing and layering in different ways. Q: Are you essentially a duo or more of a trio? I ask because I noticed that your lyrics are not always written by the two of you. Could you explain how that collaboration works, and how the lyrical themes develop in relation to your own musical ideas? Irini : Musically speaking, we’re definitely a duo; the two of us write and play all the music, and we handle everything that goes into running a band. But at the same time we also have a ‘secret’ third member. This is the poet Konstantinos Londos, whom we are lucky enough to have in our lives as a very special and dearly loved friend. He wrote the lyrics for our last two albums (with the exception of two songs, one on each record). Konstantinos puts what we feel and want to communicate into words in the most wonderful way. Working with him is magical. A lot of times we’ll discuss a topic that’s really on our minds, and then Konstantinos will write a poem about it… and just like that, we have the lyrics for a song. Other times, we picked some of his existing poems that spoke to our hearts, set them to music, and turned them into songs (like “Mutate” and “Alien Room”). But either way, there’s always an incredible creative process between the 3 of us – we listen together to the musical ideas, discuss the meaning of the lyrics, how the words flow melodically, and their deeper impact. In the end, after plenty of changes and fine-tuning (and sometimes after a lot of tears) the song finally takes its true shape. Konstantinos has a rare gift for clarity, simplicity, humor, sensitivity and working together with him is really a pleasure. He is an explosive mix of a brilliant Renaissance man, a Homo Universalis, and someone who genuinely prefers to stay out of the spotlight. Q: Speaking of the lyrics, “Trace” is an intriguing title that can be interpreted in many different ways. The album also explores profound and, at times, rather introspective themes. Could you tell us more about the concept behind the album? And to what extent do the lyrics shape the atmosphere of the music—or is it sometimes the other way around? Irini: Finding the right album title is usually a tricky process, since it needs to capture a lot of different concepts in just a few words. But with “Trace”, things were easier – the title came about completely spontaneously from Konstantinos, right after a chat about what making this album meant to us. The word means ‘imprint’; and that’s exactly what this record is: the footprint of a collaboration between people trying to capture in sounds and words the things that spark their thoughts and haunt their nights. This is also stated in the album’s back cover: “Trace”; is the imprint of ‘searching for wondrous , meaningful diversions , novel transformations  and transitory acts of care and defiance’. Thematically the songs deal with the uniqueness of human experience and the struggle of not losing one’s inner freedom and individuality in dystopian times – the ‘seeming real’; where all that is imposed and inhumane presents itself as the inevitable truth (“Always Here”). Celebrating diversity and self-expression, but always connecting and creating with other people, is a way out (“Mutate”). And the album itself is the result of such a process; we consider ourselves, against the odds, as artisans and friends who make music, share it and reinvent ourselves. Other songs cover universal, age-old themes like love, loneliness, the fear of loss, pain of death (“Sometimes”, “Region”), also the relationship with oneself and the connection with the world outside (“Diver”, “Find”), themes like the dream element, the urban landscape, and mysterious, fairy-like figures are touched upon in the songs “Alexia”, “Presence”, “She Is In The Dream”; burning issues of our time like domestic violence (“Alien Room”); and how the ‘self’ connects with today’s world, showing endless introspection but a lack of empathy, human pain, and the way we try to hide it even from ourselves (“ΚΡΥΦΟ”; – means “Hidden”); which is the only track in Greek language). George: Since songwriting is a two-way street, as we described earlier, the atmosphere that is created depends on each individual song. When we start composing music for an existing poem, we are influenced by the content, the meaning of the lyrics, and the rhythm of the words and syllables. Conversely, Konstantinos would often listen to a musical theme we had composed and write lyrics over it, based on a topic that was on our minds and that we had been discussing. However, since the general vibe of our music and lyrics is already introspective and relatively dark, we take it for granted that we won’t stray from that… not out of principle, but because the darker element simply speaks to us emotionally and temperamentally. Q: How do you approach your live performances? More specifically, how do you translate the layered studio recordings, and especially the analogue elements, to the stage? George: Βeing a duo has a lot of advantages, like flexibility with rehearsals, the creative process, and traveling. But also has plenty of challenges… Practically speaking, if we wanted to perform our tracks live with their full studio orchestration, we would definitely need at least one more musician on stage. Our compromise is to use backing tracks for the drums, or a portion of them while I play the rest, and then we perform the melodic and bass lines live. We inevitably have to skip several elements from the album… still that’s not necessarily a bad thing for a live performance, because different things take priority on stage. Also, for gigs, we bring along smaller gear. It would be practically impossible for just two people to travel carrying the actual instruments we used to compose and record, so we adapt our sound to smaller, more flexible instruments, which are a mix of analog, hybrid, and digital instruments. When we play in our hometown, things are much  easier and we can bring along some of the original (and heavy) instruments used in the recording. But when it comes to touring abroad, since we travel by plane and train, doing that would totally be out of the question for practical reasons. Irini: Over time, we’ve rearranged some tracks for our live shows to such an extent that they end up sounding quite different from the studio recordings, in terms of orchestration, tempo, and also vocals. This is especially true for songs from our first album. Also, since we love improvisation, we play the tracks a bit differently at almost every gig. We add intros, change up some riffs, and basically transform them depending on the mood of the moment. It would be really interesting at some point to make an album with our older songs exactly as they are played live, in a live recording setup. This happened already with one song , the “Only One Smile Alone”; the original one is “The Smile”; and following the suggestion of Andreas Hermann, we recorded it again in the way we play it live. Q: Finally, with an album title like “Trace”, it seems only natural to ask: what kind of trace do you hope this album—and Incirrina’s music in general—will leave behind? And what lies ahead for the band in the coming months? Ιrini: What we truly want with all our hearts is this: for people who will listen to our music, to feel something, to be moved, to dance, to feel good, or to find a personal meaning in our songs. Through our music, we aren’t seeking self-expression as much as we are seeking connection and co-motion, sharing in something as beautiful as music. We would love for the music of Incirrina to leave a small imprint of beauty in this world. Everything is fleeting and surely everything fades into the oblivion of time, but we would be incredibly happy if, even for just a few moments, we could bring joy to some people… just as we experience the joy of making songs and playing together, in rehearsals or in live shows. George: In the coming months, we will mainly focus on presenting “Trace” through live performances in Greece and Europe. We definitely want to work on producing some new songs as well, and we also plan to celebrate our 10th anniversary as a band with something special, which we will announce in early 2027…! Thank you for this interview, and we wish all the very best to you and your readers! Incirrina

items.body: Dwayne Goettel, keyboardist, sampling and programming specialist for the industrial band Skinny Puppy, died on 23 August 1995 at the age of 31. He was found dead at his parents’ home in Edmonton, Alberta, of an apparent heroin overdose. Thirty-one years on, Goettel remains one of the defining figures behind Skinny Puppy’s sound between 1986 and 1995. Dwayne Rudolph Goettel was born on 1 February 1964 in High Prairie, Alberta, Canada. A classically trained pianist, he grew up in Edmonton, where he played trumpet in his high school band before taking up piano and getting involved in the city’s small electronic music scene, including the groups Psyche and Water. He met cEvin Key in 1985 when Water opened for Skinny Puppy on their “Bites” tour. Key asked him to join the band the following year, replacing keyboardist Bill Leeb, who left to form Front Line Assembly. Goettel made his first contributions to Skinny Puppy on the album “Mind: The Perpetual Intercourse” (1986). His technical knowledge of samplers and studio equipment, particularly the Ensoniq Mirage, helped steer the band away from its early synth-pop sound toward the more abrasive, sample-driven style of “Cleanse Fold and Manipulate” (1987), “VIVIsectVI” (1988), “Rabies” (1989), “Too Dark Park” (1990) and “Last Rights” (1992). cEvin Key later credited Goettel’s early command of the technology, calling him “the master of sampling.” Alongside his work with Skinny Puppy, Goettel collaborated with Key on the side projects The Tear Garden, formed with singer Edward Ka-Spel, as well as Doubting Thomas, Hilt and Cyberaktif, which Key also shared with Bill Leeb. Goettel released solo material under the name aDuck and, in 1993, co-founded the label Subconscious Communications with Phil Western. Skinny Puppy’s eighth studio album, “The Process,” was recorded in Los Angeles beginning in 1993, but the sessions were marked by drug problems and conflict within the band. Vocalist Nivek Ogre quit in June 1995, and Goettel and Key returned to Vancouver with the master tapes. Goettel entered a rehabilitation programme in Edmonton before returning to work on Download, a side project he had started with Key. He was later readmitted to rehab. On 23 August 1995, Goettel was found dead at his parents’ home in Edmonton; his death was attributed to a heroin overdose. “The Process” was completed by Key and producer Dave “Rave” Ogilvie and released in 1996, dedicated to Goettel’s memory, as was Download’s debut album, “Furnace.” About Skinny Puppy Skinny Puppy formed in Vancouver, Canada, in 1982 as a side project for cEvin Key (born Kevin Crompton), who was also drumming in the new wave band Images in Vogue. Key recruited Nivek Ogre (Kevin Ogilvie) as vocalist, and the pair adopted stage names to avoid confusion between two members both named Kevin. The band self-released the EP “Back & Forth” in 1983 and signed to Vancouver label Nettwerk the same year. The EP “Remission” followed in December 1984, and Skinny Puppy’s debut full-length album, “Bites,” arrived in 1985. Bill Leeb, performing as Wilhelm Schroeder, joined on bass synth and backing vocals during this period. Leeb left the band in 1986 to form Front Line Assembly, and Dwayne Goettel replaced him, making his first contributions to “Mind: The Perpetual Intercourse” (1986). Skinny Puppy went on to release “Cleanse Fold and Manipulate” (1987), “VIVIsectVI” (1988) and “Rabies” (1989), the last featuring Ministry’s Al Jourgensen, followed by “Too Dark Park” (1990) and “Last Rights” (1992), the band’s final album for Nettwerk. In 1993 the group signed to Rick Rubin’s American Recordings and relocated to Los Angeles to record “The Process.” The sessions were affected by conflict and drug problems; Ogre quit in June 1995, and Goettel died two months later. Key and Dave “Rave” Ogilvie completed “The Process,” releasing it in 1996 in Goettel’s memory. Skinny Puppy reunited for a one-off performance at the Doomsday Festival in Dresden, Germany, in August 2000, leaving the keyboard station on stage empty in tribute to Goettel. The band reformed as a full-time project in 2003 with producer Mark Walk, releasing “The Greater Wrong of the Right” (2004), “Mythmaker” (2007), “HanDover” (2011) and “Weapon” (2013). In a 2023 interview, the band confirmed it had split up for good after more than four decades together. Goettel’s death on 23 August 1995 remains part of that history: 31 years on, his contribution to albums including “Too Dark Park” and “Last Rights” is remembered as central to Skinny Puppy’s sound.

items.body: Front 242 released the album “05:22:09:12 Off” on 23 August 1993 through Red Rhino Europe, with Epic issuing the record in the United States that November. The seventh studio album by the Belgian industrial/EBM group turns 33 this year. Its title is a substitution cipher spelling out the word “evil,” each letter replaced by its position in the alphabet. “05:22:09:12 Off” was produced and mixed by Daniel Bressanutti and Patrick Codenys alongside John Dubs and Eran Westwood, with Bob Ludwig mastering. The album marks the only Front 242 studio release built primarily around a guest vocalist: Kristin “99” Kowalski of the New York band Spill sings lead on most tracks, with Jean-Luc De Meyer appearing only on the remix “Melt (Again).” The CD edition runs 16 tracks, including “Animal (Cage),” “Modern Angel,” “Junkdrome,” “Serial Killers Don’t Kill Their Girlfriend,” “GenEcide” and “Crushed.” The album reached number 27 on the CMJ Radio Top 150. About Front 242 Front 242 formed in 1981 in Aarschot, near Leuven, Belgium, founded by Daniel Bressanutti (electronics, production) and Dirk Bergen (graphic design). Patrick Codenys (keyboards, programming) and vocalist Jean-Luc De Meyer joined in 1982, and Richard “23” Jonckheere (electronic percussion, backing vocals) joined in 1983 as Bergen moved into design and management. The band’s 1984 album “No Comment” was among the first releases to use the term “electronic body music” in its liner notes. Front 242 signed to Wax Trax! in the US in 1984, then released “Official Version” (1987) and “Front by Front” (1988) via Red Rhino Europe/PIAS, and “Tyranny (For You)” (1991) via Epic, its highest-charting album in the US. “05:22:09:12 Off” followed in 1993, released in Europe by Red Rhino Europe on 23 August and in the US by Epic that November. Drummer Tim Kroker joined for live performances in 2008. The band’s most recent studio album, “Pulse,” followed via XIII Bis/Metropolis in 2003. In 2023, Front 242 co-headlined the “Join The Forces” tour of Europe with Nitzer Ebb, alternating headline sets across dates including Berlin, Amsterdam, Oslo and Munich. Front 242 announced its farewell “Black Out” tour in March 2024 and played its final three shows at Ancienne Belgique in Brussels on 23-25 January 2025, retiring from live performance with a lineup of Bressanutti, De Meyer, Codenys, Richard 23 and Kroker. The live album “Black Out”, drawn from more than forty farewell-tour shows, followed via Alfa Matrix on 19 June 2026. “05:22:09:12 Off” now marks 33 years since its original release.

Despite the sheer power of this Industrial-Metal assault, there are also a few more refined Pop arrangements to be found. This makes the whole thing highly accessible, but believe me, the album remains packed with adrenaline from start to finish. There is a fine balance between the guitar work and the synths, creating a powerful and dynamic sound. Ministry fans will undoubtedly appreciate this project. “Terminal Days” sounds like a very promising debut album, and Negative Agent is undoubtedly a name to keep in mind. (Rating:7)-. items.body: August 14th was another joyous evening in New Brunswick, New Jersey, which is quickly establishing itself as a hot spot for any touring noise acts to stop through on the east coast. Considering the enthusiastic attendees and diverse local talent pool available for these shows though, this comes off as no surprise. As a result, acts of both the new and old guard are able to use this intimate basement setting as a proving ground to show their stuff to a rather open-minded but critically thinking crowd. So when Midwest noisecore legends Penis Geyser announced they would be touring in celebration of their twentieth anniversary, booking them a show in Hub City was a no-brainer. First act of the night was FRICKER, who I would put into contention as modern noise’s best kept secret anywhere. The unique blend of digital soundscape smashing and crude feedback that he brings to the table can be tailored to just about any sound system that he comes across, which leads to each live experience being different from the last. Given the grimy nature of Ferren Mall’s sound system, I figured the crowd would be in for something on the crustier side of his material. Indeed, I was right on that front. Fricker spared no room for intricacies, and immediately summoned churning rumble grumble to suck the audience into a vacuum of unforgiving sound. The feedback drone that started the set eventually gave way to more variety in the chopping of digital samples, but never once lost its harsh backing. It seems like there is not a single sound system that this red-headed prince can’t conquer, and the audience seemed to think so, as much feedback I heard after was that this set made the travel and admission price alone feel worth it. With a bar set that high, things could only go up from there. When it comes to performances I take part in, I try to often gauge how the audience is feeling about things both during and after the set. With EVIL BONG, this task is never really that hard. Being showered in a sea of audience laughter and “fuck you” cries gives you a good idea of where your performance stands. With 6 members to this unit, every full band blast came closer to sounding like harsh noise wall than perhaps a noisecore band would sound. Between takes, microphone feedback would shriek like a drunken sailor beginning to hurl as song titles that took shots at New Brunswick, the audience, the bands playing and more came out of the mouth of their jackass drummer (side note: that guy really is a jerk). By the end of the set, with the audience in a frenzy, several members of the band just began to throw themselves directly at the audience. Hey, if hurting them emotionally won’t break their spirits, why not try physically?? By the time the band finished their crowd-pleasing closer, “Fuck Scronch,” there was simply nothing more they could do than to cheer and submit to the power of Evil Bong. Much like the film series this band was named after, audiences can’t help but find entertainment in the horror of this performance. To simply shower praise towards PENIS GEYSER would not be enough to describe the masterclass their performance was. While most seasoned attendees of noise shows expect short sets, nobody was expecting just 90 seconds from this touring unit. It’s 20 years of the band, you would be more than understanding if they wanted to play a long set. Nope; 90 seconds and it’s off the stage. But in that time, the band managed to whip the audience between blasting frenzy, tense restraint and dadaist rock n roll deconstruction that would have left the most seasoned of touring acts in absolute disbelief by how disciplined the trio were in their attack. While the blasting noisecore is what most of us came for, I found myself more intrigued by the moments in between, when drummer Mikeal VanCleave would gently tap on his kit while the string slinging duo of Brad Griggs and Charlie Mumma would treat their guitars as anything other than traditional songwriting. Strings were detuned, slapped around, beaten and mangled. The frenetic energy of these actions sounded closer to someone rattling their cabinet around than actually attempting to play anything musical. And when it all finally came to an end, it wasn’t bombastic. The band simply stopped playing whatever interlude they were in the midst of and started breaking their gear down. The audience cheered for an encore. I heard “One more! One more!” cried out repeatedly (what would even be “one more” for this band? Certainly not a song). Finally, one attendee walking out said “nah, it was perfect” and left. I couldn’t have said it better myself; a phenomenal band that could go on for another 20 years and probably still be as good. The new blood of New Jersey closed the evening’s happenings, as SPLOOGE RECEPTACLE came out with a table full of gear and the enthusiasm to inject their own brand of reckless abandon onto the audience. For those maybe not in the know, this group serves as the house band for New Jersey–based record label, NJMA, which has taken on the mantle of all things absurd and limited-edition in the Garden State. There are too many projects and releases to even begin listing the “essentials,” but Splooge Receptacle is where all these insane minds come together to celebrate the power of all things noise and core. Members were switching between duties on the mic, guitar, drums, electronics, etc. Really, if someone felt like they wanted to play something more than another member at the moment, they made the switch off occur. Similar to the Evil Bong performance from earlier, Splooge also engaged in their own form of audience antagonizing, as members crashed into the crowd while raging out through the wall of sound. Even when sound was not always perfect (sorry for providing a bad cable, team), their reckless abandon carried the set a great deal. With each passing set this group does, I become more and more excited at the prospect of where their sound can go. This group will be a name to look out for in the coming years if your listening diet tends to lean towards the more lo-fi ends of noisecore and shitnoise. So with the final blastbeat sounding off, the crowd took the streets, wandering off to who-the-hell-knows until the next show. Maybe some went to the nearest eatery available. Personally speaking, I went off to the Edison Diner for some late-night nachos with the Penis Geyser crew in tow. But maybe some walked away from this one thinking of how inspiring it could be to see the most chaotic and shittiest sounds performed so excellently. I know plenty that are still buzzing days later from the whole affair.
